catalog_quote: 11. WORD STRESS. Word stress is normally penultimate. This applies to roots as well as derived forms. Other than for a particular group of words with an epenthetic final /-Vʔ/, sometimes referred to as a paragogic syllable (Sneddon 1993), described later in this section, there are very few exceptions to the Barang-barang penultimate stress rule. [p. 60] ... The major exception to the penultimate stress rule is with a group of words, often recognized as borrowings in which the original word had a final consonant. Apparently when these words were assimilated into Barang-barang, they retained the stress on the same syllable that was originally stressed, and added an paragogic final syllable /-Vʔ/ with an echo vowel. ... new_statements.rule_in_words: Primary word stress falls on the penultimate syllable of the word, for roots and for affixed/derived forms alike (stress re-computes on the affixed word). The only exception is a class of (mostly borrowed) words that originally ended in a consonant: Barang-barang adds a paragogic syllable /-Vʔ/ whose vowel echoes the root's last vowel, but stress stays on the originally stressed syllable, so these words surface with antepenultimate stress (the authors contrast this with Kaili-Pamona languages, where stress moves to the syllable before the added one).
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not mentioned in the snippets retrieved; unknown for the full section.
new_statements.exceptions: Recently assimilated loanwords with an original final consonant plus epenthetic/paragogic echo-vowel syllable /-Vʔ/ keep their original stress and therefore show antepenultimate stress (abstract and word STRESS section). Grimes & Grimes 1987 (survey wordlist) likewise treat penultimate as default and apostrophe-mark three deviant Laiyolo forms.
new_statements.domain_note: Word level ('Word stress'); explicitly covers roots and derived (affixed) forms, 'regardless of affixation'. Data are from the Barang-barang (Loa') dialect, southern Selayar, elicited by an SIL linguist with a native co-author. No phrase-level or citation-form caveats visible in the snippets.
new_statements.identity_note: The description is of Barang-barang (endonym Loa'/Lowa), spoken in Barang-barang village, Desa Lowa, on the southern tip of Selayar; Glottolog, Ethnologue and Wikipedia treat Barang-Barang as a dialect/variety of Laiyolo [lji, laiy1246] with no separate glottocode. Grimes & Grimes (1987:61) record two dialects, Laiyolo and Barang-Barang, whose speakers report 'differences of vocabulary and intonation'; the stress statement should be filed for laiy1246 with the dialect noted as Barang-barang.
